## Context

Certified unlearning [@guo2020certified; @sekhari2021remember] asks the output of
an unlearning algorithm $\U$ to be indistinguishable from *retraining from
scratch* on the retain set. Write $\mu \approx_{\varepsilon,\delta} \nu$ for
$(\varepsilon,\delta)$-indistinguishability of two output distributions.

::: {#def-classical name="certified unlearning (retraining reference)"}

For every $\D$ and every partition $\D = \Dr \sqcup \Df$,

$$
\U\bigl(\A(\D),\, \Dr,\, \Df\bigr) \;\approx_{\varepsilon,\delta}\; \A(\Dr).
$$ {#eq-classical}

:::

This is presented as the unlearning analogue of differential privacy
[@dwork2006calibrating]. It is not.

## Idea

> The retrained model is not the released model minus $z$. It is the released
> model minus $z$ **and** minus the unlearning procedure. Comparing against it
> charges that procedure gap to $z$'s privacy budget.

Fix a forget point $z \in \Df$, let $z'$ be another record put in its place, and
write $\D^{z\to z'}$ for the dataset with the swap applied. Three distributions
over released models:

$$
\underbrace{\U\bigl(\A(\D),\Dr,\Df\bigr)}_{P:\ \text{model saw } z}
\qquad
\underbrace{\U\bigl(\A(\D^{z\to z'}),\Dr,\Df^{z\to z'}\bigr)}_{Q:\ \text{model saw } z' \text{ instead, same procedure}}
\qquad
\underbrace{\A(\Dr)}_{R:\ \text{no } z, \text{ different procedure}}
$$ {#eq-three}

What the release says about $z$ is the $P$ / $Q$ gap: one mechanism, one record
swapped. @eq-classical constrains the $P$ / $R$ gap instead, and $P$ and $R$
differ in two ways at once — by the record *and* by the procedure that produced
them. So any test separating $P$ from $R$ reports a mixture of two signals.

The second signal is the $Q$ / $R$ gap: how far *unlearning a dataset that never
contained $z$* is from *training on that same dataset from scratch*. It has
nothing to do with $z$. For any inexact $\U$ it is non-zero, and it does not
shrink as the leakage about $z$ shrinks — it is still there when there is
nothing at all to leak. This is a **bias of learning procedure**, not noise, and
it can push the answer either way.

Removing it costs one change: put $Q$ where $R$ was, so the two worlds differ by
the record and nothing else.

::: {#def-rectified name="rectified certified unlearning"}

For every $\D$, every partition $\D = \Dr \sqcup \Df$, every $z \in \Df$ and
every replacement $z'$,

$$
\U\bigl(\A(\D),\, \Dr,\, \Df\bigr)
\;\approx_{\varepsilon,\delta}\;
\U\bigl(\A(\D^{z\to z'}),\, \Dr,\, \Df^{z\to z'}\bigr).
$$ {#eq-rectified}

:::

Two design choices in that statement are worth spelling out.

**Swap, not delete.** Differential privacy in its bounded form compares datasets
of *equal size*; building the definition on deletion would make the two worlds
differ in size as well as in content, which is one more asymmetry to account for.
Here $z'$ takes $z$'s slot inside $\Df$, so both worlds have the same $|\D|$, the
same $|\Dr|$ and the same $|\Df|$. The comparison is about *which* record was
processed, never about how many. This is also what the audits do: LiRA-style
shadow-model populations [@carlini2022membership] are built at fixed training-set
size, so the empirical IN and OUT worlds already differ by a swap, not by a
deletion.

**Worst case in the definition, sampled in the audit.** @def-rectified
quantifies over all pairs $(z, z')$, as a neighbouring relation should. An
attack cannot: it instantiates $z'$ by drawing a fresh record from the data
distribution, one the model never saw. That is precisely what a held-out pool is
for.

Sanity check: take $\U$ to be the identity. @def-rectified collapses to
$\A(\D) \approx_{\varepsilon,\delta} \A(\D^{z\to z'})$ — plain bounded
differential privacy of the learner at $z$. Doing no unlearning at all is
admissible exactly when the model was already private, which is what a privacy
condition should say.

The same bias sits in the audits, and this is where the rectified definition
already has an empirical counterpart. U-LiRA and its descendants
[@hayes2024inexact] score unlearned models against *retrained* shadow models:
the measured ROC separates $P$ from $R$, so a record with no leakage at all
still scores whatever procedure gap the algorithm carries.
RULI [@naderloui2025ruli] is the framework that removes it. Its **Game 2** fixes
an adversary-chosen target set *before* unlearning, then asks whether a target
$z$ was trained-then-unlearned or never trained — both worlds releasing the same
$\U\circ\A$, only the identity of the record changing. That is @eq-rectified,
with the procedure held fixed and the bias cancelled by construction.

Two claims come out of this, and they should not be confused. As a
**guarantee**, @def-classical is sound: @prp-sufficient below shows it implies
the per-record statement up to a factor of two. It is merely stronger than
needed. As a **measurement**, the $P$ / $R$ statistic is biased, with no
determined sign. The second claim is the one worth making.

## Formalisation

### Rectified versus classical

::: {#prp-sufficient name="the retraining model is a pivot"}

@def-classical at $(\varepsilon,\delta)$ implies @def-rectified at
$\bigl(2\varepsilon,\,(1+e^{\varepsilon})\delta\bigr)$.

:::

*Proof.* Swapping inside $\Df$ leaves the retain set untouched, so @def-classical
applied to $\D$ and to $\D^{z\to z'}$ bounds $(P,R)$ and $(Q,R)$ against the
**same** $R$; conclude by the triangle inequality. $\square$

Note what the second instance is: it asks $Q \approx R$, i.e. that unlearning a
$z$-free dataset be indistinguishable from training on it. @def-classical does
not correct the procedure bias — it forbids it outright. That is why it is
sufficient, and also why it asks more than protecting $z$ requires.

The pivot exists only because $z$ is a forget point. For $z \in \Dr$ the
references are $\A(\Dr)$ and $\A(\Dr^{z\to z'})$, and @eq-classical says nothing
— protecting retain points is $\A$'s job.

There is **no converse**, and the size-preserving form is what kills it. A
deletion-based definition would let one peel forget points off one at a time
until $\Df$ is empty and the state is $\A(\Dr)$, recovering @def-classical by
group privacy at group size $|\Df|$. Swapping never empties $\Df$, so no chain of
neighbours reaches $\A(\Dr)$ at all. Nor does any other route: a $\U$ that
releases the model together with a noisy aggregate over $\Df$ satisfies
@def-rectified with small $\varepsilon$ — one swap moves the aggregate by a
bounded amount — while failing @def-classical outright, since $R$ carries no such
coordinate. @def-classical is strictly stronger, and the gap is not a factor of
$|\Df|$: it is the procedure requirement, which @def-rectified does not express.

### The data space has to change

Now try to write @def-rectified as $M(D) \approx M(D')$. The obstruction is
immediate: $\U\circ\A$ is not a function of a dataset. It takes three arguments,
and the partition $(\Dr,\Df)$ is an extra input channel — same $\D$, different
forget request, different output law. There is no mechanism on
$\mathcal{Z}^{*}$ to apply DP to.

Move the channel into the records. With
$\mathcal{Z} = \mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{Y}$, put

$$
\tilde{\mathcal{Z}} \;=\; \mathcal{X} \times \mathcal{Y} \times \{\mathsf{r},\mathsf{f}\},
$$ {#eq-augmented}

so an **unlearning-aware dataset** $\tilde\D \in \tilde{\mathcal{Z}}^{*}$ is data,
labels, *and* each record's retain/forget status. Writing $\pi,\pi_{\mathsf r},
\pi_{\mathsf f}$ for the three projections, the single randomised mechanism

$$
M(\tilde\D) \;=\; \U\bigl(\A(\pi\tilde\D),\, \pi_{\mathsf r}\tilde\D,\, \pi_{\mathsf f}\tilde\D\bigr)
$$ {#eq-mechanism}

*is* a mechanism on a dataset, and @def-rectified is literally
$M(\tilde\D) \approx_{\varepsilon,\delta} M(\tilde\D')$ for $\tilde\D'$ obtained
by replacing one $\mathsf f$-record with another.

### One relation, three cases

Here is what the typing costs. On $\tilde{\mathcal{Z}}^{*}$, DP's neighbouring
relation — *differ in a single record* — no longer has one case but three,
because a record now carries a status. Two of them keep the status fixed,

$$
\tilde\D \sim_{\mathsf f} \tilde\D'
\;:\; (x,y,\mathsf f) \rightarrow (x',y',\mathsf f),
\qquad
\tilde\D \sim_{\mathsf r} \tilde\D'
\;:\; (x,y,\mathsf r) \rightarrow (x',y',\mathsf r),
$$ {#eq-neighbours}

and the third changes it: the **relabel** $\sim_{\mathsf{rel}}$, which keeps
$(x,y)$ and flips $\mathsf r \leftrightarrow \mathsf f$. These three generate the
whole relation — a general one-record change with a status flip factors as a
relabel followed by a same-status swap.

Give all three the same budget and $M$ is ordinarily differentially private on
$\tilde{\mathcal{Z}}^{*}$; this is why a DP learner unlearns for free. The
unlearning regime is the one that does not: @def-rectified constrains
$\sim_{\mathsf f}$ alone. Call $M$
$(\varepsilon_{\mathsf f},\varepsilon_{\mathsf r})$-private when it is
$\varepsilon_{\mathsf f}$-indistinguishable across $\sim_{\mathsf f}$ and
$\varepsilon_{\mathsf r}$-indistinguishable across $\sim_{\mathsf r}$. Then
$\varepsilon_{\mathsf f}$ small with $\varepsilon_{\mathsf r} = \infty$ is
unlearning and nothing else, and
$\varepsilon_{\mathsf f} \ll \varepsilon_{\mathsf r} < \infty$ is the interesting
regime.

> Unlearning is not a weaker privacy notion. It is differential privacy on a
> typed data space with an **asymmetric budget** across record types.

Per-record budgets are not new — personalized differential privacy
[@jorgensen2015conservative] and its descendants have assigned heterogeneous
$\varepsilon$ for a decade. What is specific here is *what* the typing is: the
unlearning status, which is not an external annotation about a data subject but
an **input the mechanism reads**, since $\U$ is a function of $\Df$.

### The status cannot be both protected and useful

The third case is the one left unconstrained above, and it is not free to
constrain. Suppose $\sim_{\mathsf{rel}}$ were protected at level
$\varepsilon_{\mathsf{rel}}$ — an observer could not tell whether $z$ had been
kept or forgotten. Compose the generators, relabel then swap then relabel back:

$$
M(\tilde\D_{z:\mathsf r})
\;\approx_{\varepsilon_{\mathsf{rel}}}\; M(\tilde\D_{z:\mathsf f})
\;\approx_{\varepsilon_{\mathsf f}}\; M(\tilde\D_{z':\mathsf f})
\;\approx_{\varepsilon_{\mathsf{rel}}}\; M(\tilde\D_{z':\mathsf r}),
$$ {#eq-chain}

whose endpoints are a $\sim_{\mathsf r}$ pair. So

$$
\varepsilon_{\mathsf r} \;\le\; \varepsilon_{\mathsf f} + 2\,\varepsilon_{\mathsf{rel}}.
$$ {#eq-price}

@eq-price prices status confidentiality in units of retain privacy, and the three
ways of reading it do not sit together comfortably.

*Make the status public* ($\varepsilon_{\mathsf{rel}} = \infty$). The asymmetry
survives and unlearning is a notion distinct from DP. This is also what
auditability wants: verifying that a request was honoured requires knowing who
asked [@thudi2022necessity]. But it means publishing, for each subject, whether
they demanded erasure.

*Protect the status* ($\varepsilon_{\mathsf{rel}} \to 0$). Then
$\varepsilon_{\mathsf r} \le \varepsilon_{\mathsf f}$: every record is protected
at the forget budget, $M$ is differentially private outright, and unlearning buys
nothing that DP training would not have bought. The asymmetry that made the
notion interesting is exactly what dies.

*Pay for it* (intermediate $\varepsilon_{\mathsf{rel}}$). The gap between the two
budgets is capped at $2\varepsilon_{\mathsf{rel}}$. Status confidentiality is
neither free nor cheap: it is bought at twice its own rate out of the retain
budget.

The uncomfortable part is that the legal setting motivating all of this pushes
towards the second horn. Under a right-to-erasure regime, *having requested
erasure* is itself personal data about the subject, and often more revealing than
dataset membership — it can signal that the person considers the record harmful
to them. The regime where unlearning is formally distinct from differential
privacy is the regime where that signal is published.

## Scope

Two things this does not do.

It is **static**. @def-rectified fixes one partition and one release. Real
deployments republish after each request, and requesters choose what to delete
after seeing the previous models; @gupta2021adaptive show that non-adaptive
deletion guarantees do not automatically compose in that setting. Nothing here
addresses it.

It buys **confidentiality, not control**. @def-classical forbids any channel
about $\Df$ beyond what retraining leaks, which is none. @def-rectified only
forbids per-record leakage — the noisy-aggregate mechanism above is the witness.
Whether that is acceptable is a normative question, not a technical one, and
there is a line of work arguing it is not: deletion-compliance by simulation
against a world where the data was never supplied [@garg2020formalizing], and
deletion-as-control as a requirement distinct from confidentiality
[@cohen2023control]. Rectifying the *metric* does not settle the *right*.

And the diagnosis is not unprecedented. @chourasia2023forget also reject the
retraining reference, on adaptivity grounds rather than as a measurement bias.
